Azure Cloud-Native Platform Updates

Follow meaningful documentation updates across Microsoft's Azure cloud-native platform, spanning container orchestration and fleet management (AKS, AKS Automatic, Application Network, AKS Support, AKS Arc, Azure Arc-enabled Kubernetes, and Kubernetes Fleet Manager), container registry (Azure Container Registry), application networking (Application Gateway for Containers), and Azure Linux. The tracker also summarizes the latest five AKS and Application Network releases.

It automatically scans for changes, then uses AI to summarize and highlight updates that are most likely to matter — such as new features, deprecations, and significant content revisions.

Minor edits (like typos, formatting tweaks, and other low-impact changes) are usually filtered out. Because the process is automated, some updates may be missed or summaries may not capture every nuance.

For complete accuracy, you can always follow the provided links to the original Microsoft documentation.

With this tracker, you can:

  • Quickly scan meaningful AKS, AKS Automatic, AKS Support, App Net, Arc K8s, AKS Arc, Azure Linux, ACR, AGC, and Fleet documentation changes from the past 7 days
  • Stay up to date with the latest AKS and App Net release notes without digging through every doc page
  • Search and browse CVE security data across AKS releases and VHD node images, powered by the AKS Vulnerability Data API (Public Preview)

Get the Latest AKS Docs - Every Week, in Your Inbox

Release 2026-10-25

AKS
View Release
📅 2026-10-27

The release on 2026-10-25 introduces automatic upgrades for unsupported Kubernetes versions and updates to node pools.

❌

Breaking Changes

  • AKS will automatically upgrade unsupported clusters after a grace period.
  • Default OS SKU for node pools changes to Ubuntu 26.04 with Kubernetes 1.38.
🔑

Key Features

  • Kubernetes 1.37 is now generally available as Long-Term Support.
  • Node Auto Provisioning (NAP) enhancements include new CRDs and features.
💡

Good to Know

  • Review upgrade channels to prepare for automated upgrades.
  • Community support for Kubernetes 1.34 ends by November 2026.

Release Notes 2026-09-25

AKS
View Release
📅 2026-10-01

The 2026-09-25 release introduces significant updates and deprecations. Key features include the general availability of identity bindings and preview support for Ubuntu 26.04.

❌

Breaking Changes

  • Windows Server 2022 is not supported in Kubernetes version 1.37 and above.
  • Flatcar Container Linux node images are removed, affecting scaling operations.
  • The annotation service.beta.kubernetes.io/azure-pip-tags no longer overrides public IP tags.
🔑

Key Features

  • Identity bindings are now generally available.
  • Ubuntu 26.04 is available in preview.
  • Windows Server OS SKU migration to 2025 is in preview.
💡

Good to Know

  • AKS will auto-migrate deprecated Availability Sets clusters after September 30, 2026.
  • AKS release order has been updated for Central US and East US.
  • Check AKS Release Tracker for detailed release timing.

Release 2026-09-04

AKS
View Release
📅 2026-09-09

This release introduces Kubernetes 1.37 and autoscaling for VM node pools. It also announces the retirement of Azure Linux with OS Guard.

❌

Breaking Changes

  • AKS will remove Azure Linux with OS Guard node images on March 10, 2027.
  • AKS no longer produces VHDs for Windows Server 2019 and version 23H2.
🔑

Key Features

  • Autoscaling for Virtual Machines node pools is now generally available.
  • Kubernetes patch versions 1.36.3, 1.35.7, and 1.34.10 are available.
  • On-Demand Monitor for node health checks is in preview.
💡

Good to Know

  • LocalDNS is enabled automatically for compatible cluster networking.
  • AKS rejects updates that remove IPv6 from dual-stack clusters.
  • Managed namespace creation rejects names starting with reserved prefixes.

Support for Azure Linux with OS Guard in Azure Kubernetes Service will end on December 10, 2026. Azure Container Linux is the replacement for Azure Linux with OS Guard (preview). Starting on December 10, 2026: - Users won’t be able to create new Azure Linux with OS Guard (preview) node pools. - AKS won’t produce new node images for affected node pools. - Existing node pools won’t receive security patches. On March 10, 2027, AKS will remove the Azure Linux with OS Guard node images. After the images are removed, scaling and remediation operations, including reimage and redeploy operations, will fail for affected node pools. You can use either of the following migration options: - Migrate an existing Azure Linux with OS Guard node pool in place by following the Migrate nodes to Azure Container Linux for Azure Kubernetes Service documentation. This operation preforms a standard node image upgrade. - Alternatively, create a new Azure Container Linux node pool, migrate and validate workloads, and then delete the Azure Linux with OS Guard node pool. Follow Add Azure Container Linux node pools and remove existing node pools. For other available options, see the AKS node operating system. If you have questions, get answers from community experts in Microsoft Q&A or AKS GitHub Repository. If you have a support plan and need technical help, create a support request.

Ubuntu 20.04 has been replaced by newer supported versions, including Ubuntu 22.04 and Ubuntu 24.04. We encourage you to transition to Ubuntu 22.04+ before the retirement date. If you’re currently using Ubuntu 20.04 with Federal Information Process Standard (FIPS) on AKS, follow our instructions to upgrade your Kubernetes version to 1.34+ where Ubuntu 22.04 will be the default Ubuntu version for FIPS workloads. To avoid service disruptions, scaling restrictions, and remain supported, please follow our instructions to upgrade your Kubernetes version to 1.34+ by March 17, 2027. On March 31, 2027 Azure Monitor will be deprecating the sidecar for remote-write of Prometheus metrics to Azure Monitor Workspace. This is as part of our ongoing efforts to improve reliability and reduce complexity. We recommend configuring your self-hosted Prometheus or Prometheus Operator to remote-write directly to Azure Monitor Workspace. All authentication methods are supported in the Prometheus remote-write configuration, and direct remote-write is fully compatible with the Prometheus Operator. You can find detailed configuration guidance in the official documentation. This approach removes the need for the sidecar and simplifies your setup. We encourage you to transition to direct Prometheus remote-write as soon as possible to take advantage of the improved experience and ensure uninterrupted service. If you have any questions or need assistance during this transition, please feel free to contact ciprometheus@microsoft.com with your name, company name, email contact and subscription IDs.

On June 30, 2027, we'll retire Ubuntu 22.04 on Azure Kubernetes Service. To avoid disruptions, transition to Ubuntu 24.04 or later by that date. Newer supported versions include kernel updates and security improvements. Until June 30, 2027, you can continue to use Ubuntu 22.04 on AKS without disruption. If you don't migrate by June 30, 2027, you won't be able to create new node pools, AKS won't produce new node images, and you'll no longer receive security patches for existing node pools. On April 30, 2028 AKS will remove Ubuntu 22.04 node images and existing code, causing scaling and remediation operations to fail. Migration Options: - Default Operating System SKU (OSSku): If you're using 'Ubuntu,' you'll automatically migrate to Ubuntu 24.04 when you upgrade your Kubernetes version to 1.35 or later. - Versioned OSSku: If you're using 'Ubuntu2204,' update your OSSku to 'Ubuntu' for Kubernetes 1.35 or later, or 'Ubuntu2404' for Kubernetes 1.32 or later. Read moreRead less
Beginning September 30, 2027, support for the pod name dimension on the following Azure Monitor platform metrics is retiring, and these metrics are transitioning to aggregate pod counters: - Number of pods by phase (kube_pod_status_phase) - Number of pods in Ready state (kube_pod_status_ready) After this change: - Metric names remain unchanged. - Aggregate pod counts remain available. - Namespace-level monitoring scenarios remain supported. - The pod name dimension will no longer be available for filtering, grouping, or alerting. During the deprecation period, AKS will maintain both the existing and the new aggregate implementations. Both are populated with data, existing monitoring experiences will continue to function, and you will have at least one year of historical data in the aggregate implementation before retirement. You may be affected if any dashboard, workbook, alert, automation, or monitoring workflow: - Uses kube_pod_status_phase or kube_pod_status_ready and filters on the pod name dimension. - Splits or groups results by the pod name dimension. Recommended action: - If you use aggregate pod counts, no action is required. - If you use the pod name dimension, update dashboards, alerts, workbooks, and automation before September 30, 2027. For pod-level monitoring and troubleshooting, we recommend using Azure Monitor Managed Prometheus and Kubernetes-native pod metrics. Help and support If you have questions, get answers from community experts in Microsoft Q&A.

Read moreRead less
The Azure Key Vault Secrets Provider Extension for Azure Arc-enabled Kubernetes will be retired on October 9, 2027. Customers currently using the extension should plan to migrate to the Azure Key Vault Secret Store Extension before the retirement date. The Azure Key Vault Secret Store Extension provides equivalent functionality for accessing and synchronizing secrets from Azure Key Vault for workloads running on Azure Arc-enabled Kubernetes clusters. In addition, the Azure Key Vault Secret Store Extension includes enhancements such as support for offline access to secrets and authentication using workload identity federation, enabling applications to access Azure Key Vault without storing long-lived credentials on the cluster. After retirement, the Azure Key Vault Secrets Provider Extension will no longer receive new features, bug fixes, security updates, or technical support. Migration guidance is available to help customers transition their workloads and configurations to the Azure Key Vault Secret Store Extension ahead of retirement.

Azure Container Registry (ACR) implements Docker Content Trust (DCT), allowing image publishers to sign their images and image consumers to verify that the images they pull are signed. With advancements in technology, Docker Content Trust no longer meets the requirements of modern supply chain security for containers. As a result, Docker Content Trust will be deprecated and no longer available in ACR after March 31, 2028. If you currently use Docker Content Trust, you should transition to the Notary Project ecosystem, including their open-source supply chain tool, Notation. How does this affect me? - Starting September 30, 2025, customers will no longer be able to enable Docker Content Trust on Azure Container Registry. - Data stored in Azure Container Registry for signing and verifying signatures with Docker Content Trust will be permanently deleted on March 31, 2028. - Docker Content Trust function will be completely removed from Azure Container Registry on March 31, 2028. Required Action Start your transition to Notary Project today and enhance the security and trust of your container ecosystem. Use the following articles to get started. Signing: - Use AKV with self-signed certificates - Use AKV with CA-issued certificates - Sign in ADO pipelines - Sign in GitHub workflows Verification: - Verify in ADO pipelines - Verify in GitHub workflows - Verify on AKS

Read moreRead less
Azure Linux 2.0 on AKS will be retired on November 30, 2025, please transition to Azure Linux 3.0 by that date. Azure Linux 2.0 has been replaced by the newer supported version Azure Linux 3.0. We encourage you to transition to Azure Linux 3.0 prior to the retirement date to experience the capabilities of Azure Linux 3.0 including kernel updates and security improvements. From now to November 30, 2025, you can continue to use Azure Linux 2.0 without disruption. On November 30, 2025, Azure Linux 2.0 will no longer be supported on AKS; AKS will no longer create new node pools, produce new node images, or provide security updates for Azure Linux 2.0 after that date. On March 31, 2026, Azure Linux 2.0 node images will be removed. This will cause scaling operations to fail. Customers can transition to Azure Linux 3.0 by taking one of the following actions: - If you’re currently using Azure Linux 2.0 on AKS, please follow our instructions to upgrade your Kubernetes version to 1.32+. - Alternately, starting Kubernetes version 1.28+ you can perform an in-place node pool update from --os-sku AzureLinux to --os-sku AzureLinux3, enabling you to migrate existing node pools from Azure Linux 2.0 to 3.0 while remaining on the same k8s version. Your node pool will automatically reimage to the equivalent Azure Linux 3.0 node image. See documentation here. To avoid service disruptions, please follow our instructions to migrate to Azure Linux 3.0 by November 30, 2025.

                                    @@ -1,4 +1,4 @@-# Azure Container Linux (ACL) for Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) Overview | Microsoft Learn+# Azure Container Linux (ACL) for Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) overview | Microsoft Learn  In this article, we provide an overview of Azure Container Linux (ACL), an immutable, container-optimized operating system (OS) for Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS). ACL is derived from the Flatcar Container Linux project, building on Flatcar's proven, container-first immutable design while layering in Azure Linux packages, servicing, and platform integration. This allows ACL to stay closely aligned with upstream Flatcar innovation while meeting Azure's production, security, and compliance requirements. To learn more about Flatcar Container Linux, see the [Flatcar documentation](https://www.flatcar.org/). @@ -10,26 +10,24 @@ Starting on **December 10, 2026**, Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) no longer supp  ## Benefits of using ACL on AKS +ACL is a secure, minimal OS that includes only the critical components required to run containers. It uses an immutable design to preserve OS integrity and reduce node configuration drift.+ | Benefit | Description | | --- | --- |-| **Built-in immutability for stronger security** | Kernel-enforced immutability of the `/usr` directory verifies the integrity of the OS image at boot and runtime. This design helps block unauthorized changes before they can affect your cluster and reduces the risk of OS-level tampering. |-| **Minimal attack surface** | ACL ships only the components required to run containers. By reducing the size and complexity of the OS, ACL minimizes the number of packages, services, and potential entry points available to attackers and simplifies security management. |-| **Automated node image updates** | ACL delivers weekly image-based updates that include the latest security patches and bug fixes. This approach keeps node OS versions consistent and current across the cluster and helps reduce exposure to known vulnerabilities. |-| **Supply-chain trust** | Builds on Azure Linux’s signed packages and supply-chain processes, delivering clear provenance for system components. |-| **Integration with Azure security features** | Native support for [Trusted Launch](/en-us/azure/aks/use-trusted-launch) and Secure Boot provides measured boot protections and attestation. |+| **Layered OS security** | ACL combines an immutable OS, mandatory access controls, verified boot, and trusted build processes to protect nodes from boot through runtime. For details, see [ACL security features](azure-container-linux-security-features). |+| **Minimal container host** | ACL includes only the components required to run containers, reducing OS complexity and simplifying node management. |+| **Consistent node servicing** | Weekly image-based updates provide security patches and bug fixes while keeping the OS version consistent across each node image. | | **Open-source transparency** | Flatcar as well as many of the underlying technologies (dm-verity and SELinux) are upstream or open source, and Microsoft has tooling and contributions to support these features. | -## Key features of ACL+## Capabilities and compatibility -The following key features distinguish ACL as a hardened, container-optimized OS for AKS:+ACL supports the following AKS capabilities: -- **Immutability**: The '/usr' directory is mounted as a read-only volume protected by dm-verity. At runtime, the kernel validates a signed root hash to detect and block tampering-- **Mandatory access control with SELinux**: ACL includes SELinux to enforce mandatory access control policies that restrict which processes can access sensitive system resources. SELinux operates in enforcing mode by default.-- **Trusted Launch and Secure Boot**: ACL requires [Trusted Launch](/en-us/azure/virtual-machines/trusted-launch) with Secure Boot and vTPM, to ensure the integrity of the boot chain before the OS loads. This is achieved using a Unified Kernel Image (UKI), which bundles the kernel, initramfs, and kernel command line into a single signed artifact. During boot, the UKI is measured and recorded in the vTPM, ensuring integrity from the earliest stage. - **NVIDIA GPU node support**: ACL supports NVIDIA GPU-enabled node pools on AMD64 architectures, allowing you to run high-performance computing (HPC) and AI/ML workloads on AKS with a hardened, container-optimized OS. ACL doesn't support ARM64 architectures for GPU-enabled node pools.+- **FIPS**: ACL supports FIPS-enabled node pools. - **AMD64 and ARM64 architecture support**: ACL is available for both AMD64 and ARM64 architectures on AKS.-- **Sovereign Supply Chain Security**: ACL inherits Azure Linux’s secure build pipelines and signed Unified Kernel Images (UKIs). - **[Node auto-provisioning](/en-us/azure/aks/node-auto-provisioning)**: ACL supports node auto-provisioning (NAP).+- **[Confidential VM](/en-us/azure/aks/use-cvm)**: ACL is available as a confidential VM (CVM) image for AKS, with a FIPS-enabled option.  ## Unsupported features

They extend the service defaults without removing them or changing the 30-second aggregation interval. Can include IPs, labels, namespace/pod selectors, and numeric identities. | No |+| `includefilters[].to` | Endpoint | Destination of the network flow. Layer 7 (HTTP, gRPC, Kafka) and DNS records show up only when matching traffic is also covered by a Cilium network policy that opts into L7 inspection or DNS visibility. Without that policy, L7 and DNS fields stay empty in your flow logs.+| `Endpoint.labelSelector` | Object | Label-based endpoint selection. Use one `matchLabels` entry or one `matchExpressions` condition per endpoint; see the multiple-condition limitation above. | No |+| `Endpoint.namespacedPod` | []string | Exact namespace and pod-name prefix in `namespace/pod` format. Use `namespace/` for all pods in that namespace. | No |+| `Endpoint.identities` | []integer | Numeric Cilium security identities from `0` through `16777215`. Keep business-critical data on durable storage such as Azure Disk or Azure Files. +## Use distributed accelerator for cloud storage (preview)++>+> **Best practice guidance**+>+> Consider distributed accelerator for cloud storage (DACS) when applications repeatedly read model files or datasets from Azure Blob Storage. Plan cache capacity, warm-up, and recovery around your workload's access patterns.++DACS uses local NVMe disks across Linux cache nodes to cache Azure Blob data. It can reduce model-loading time for AI inference and accelerate repeated dataset reads for training. You enable and manage DACS through Azure Container Storage. DACS doesn't provision persistent volumes or storage classes.++When you plan and operate DACS:++- **Dedicate cache storage.** Use Linux cache nodes with local NVMe disks dedicated to DACS. Cache prerequisites can format those disks. Preserve cache-node labels in the node-pool configuration so they survive node replacement.+- **Size for the active working set.** Include headroom for overlapping model versions and dataset changes. Account for concurrent readers, node CPU and memory, and network bandwidth, not just NVMe capacity.+- **Plan for cold reads.** Consider prefetching model data before inference deployments or scale-out. Verify cache hits before increasing concurrency. Prefetch doesn't pin data, and eviction, node replacement, or maintenance can require another warm-up. Plan for additional Blob traffic when cached data is unavailable.+- **Measure application and cache behavior.** Compare cold and warm reads under expected concurrency. Monitor client cache hits, cache-server requests, latency, capacity, and Blob traffic. Successful or faster reads alone don't prove cache use because clients can fall back to Azure Blob Storage.+- **Keep authoritative data durable.** Store model files and datasets in Azure Blob Storage, preferably at immutable, versioned paths. Cached data is ephemeral and isn't replicated for durability. Don't use DACS as persistent storage for training outputs or checkpoints.++Important++DACS is in preview. If you can't [remove state from your applications](operator-best-practices-multi-region#remove-service-state-from-inside-containers), back up the data from persistent volumes and regularly test the restore operations to verify data integrity and the processes required. In some scenarios, pods that communicate with one another can be in different node pools.+In scenarios that involve multiple node pools, you can put the pods in the `kube-system` namespace on one node pool (the system node pool) while you put the application pods on a different node pool (the user node pool). For more information, see [Associate or dissociate a network security group to or from a subnet or network interface](/en-us/azure/virtual-network/manage-network-security-group#associate-or-dissociate-a-network-security-group-to-or-from-a-subnet-or-network-interface).-- If you're using an App Service plan with a subnet connected to the AKS cluster's VNET, you have to remove the associated App Service plan and its internal resources (such as Function App and SQL Azure database) and then retry deleting the AKS cluster.+- If you're using an Azure App Service plan with a subnet connected to the AKS cluster's virtual network (VNET), you must remove the associated App Service plan and its internal resources (such as Azure Functions and Azure SQL Database) and then retry deleting the AKS cluster.

Each workload requests `nvidia.com/gpu`, where one unit represents one partition rather than an entire physical GPU. AKS installs and configures the NVIDIA driver and device plugin for this path. For strategy selection and resource naming, see [Multi-instance GPU strategies in AKS](multi-instance-gpu-overview). Inventory the current pool's VM size, `gpuInstanceProfile`, node image, and advertised partition capacity. Record workload selectors, affinity, taints, tolerations, and GPU requests. Check whether the existing NVIDIA device plugin or GPU operator serves other node pools.+2. Ensure that your self-managed NVIDIA device plugin and any GPU operator don't reconcile the replacement MIG pool's nodes. Replace the resource ID, VM size, and zone with values for your reservation.++```yaml+    apiVersion: karpenter.azure.com/v1beta1+    kind: AKSNodeClass+    metadata:+      name: reserved+    spec:+      capacityReservation:+        groupID: /subscriptions/<subscription-id>/resourceGroups/<crg-resource-group>/providers/Microsoft.Compute/capacityReservationGroups/<crg-name>+```++For a regional, zone-less member, replace the `topology.kubernetes.io/zone` requirement with:++```yaml+- key: karpenter.azure.com/placement-scope+  operator: In+  values: ["regional"]+```++Important++The association is a launch constraint, not a preference: every node you launch from this class targets the group. Nodes remain labeled `karpenter.sh/capacity-type: on-demand`; don't use `reserved` as a capacity type.                                                                                                                                                                                                     @@ -2,51 +2,47 @@  In this article, we provide an overview of Azure Container Linux (ACL), an immutable, container-optimized operating system (OS) for Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS). ACL is derived from the Flatcar Container Linux project, building on Flatcar's proven, container-first immutable design while layering in Azure Linux packages, servicing, and platform integration. This allows ACL to stay closely aligned with upstream Flatcar innovation while meeting Azure's production, security, and compliance requirements. To learn more about Flatcar Container Linux, see the [Flatcar documentation](https://www.flatcar.org/). -ACL is generally available (GA) as an OS option on AKS starting AKS v1.34. You can deploy ACL node pools in a new AKS cluster, add ACL node pools to your existing clusters, and migrate existing Linux node pools to ACL.+ACL is generally available (GA) as an OS option on AKS starting AKS v1.34. You can deploy ACL node pools in a new AKS cluster or add ACL node pools to your existing clusters. -Note+Important -ACL is the GA release of Flatcar Container Linux for AKS, which entered preview in November 2025. OS Guard (preview) features, such as code integrity with Integrity Policy Enforcement (IPE), currently aren't supported. If you need OS Guard features today, we recommend continuing to use OS Guard and migrating to ACL once those features become available.+Starting on **December 10, 2026**, Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) no longer supports Azure Linux with OS Guard for AKS (preview). At that point, AKS no longer produces new Azure Linux with OS Guard node images or provides security patches, and you can no longer create new node pools with Azure Linux with OS Guard. On **March 10, 2027**, AKS removes all existing Azure Linux with OS Guard node images, which causes scaling and remediation (reimage and redeploy) operations to fail. To avoid disruption, migrate to [Azure Container Linux (ACL)](azure-container-linux-overview). For more information about this retirement, see the [Retirement GitHub issue](https://github.com/Azure/AKS/issues/5950) and the [Azure Updates retirement announcement](https://azure.microsoft.com/updates/?id=571257). To stay informed about announcements and updates, follow the [AKS release notes](https://github.com/Azure/AKS/releases).  ## Benefits of using ACL on AKS -Using ACL as the OS for your AKS node pools provides several benefits that enhance security, reliability, and operational efficiency:+ACL is a secure, minimal OS that includes only the critical components required to run containers. It uses an immutable design to preserve OS integrity and reduce node configuration drift. -- **Built-in immutability for stronger security**: Kernel-enforced immutability of the `/usr` directory verifies the integrity of the OS image at boot and runtime. This design helps block unauthorized changes before they can affect your cluster and reduces the risk of OS-level tampering.-- **Minimal attack surface**: ACL ships only the components required to run containers. By reducing the size and complexity of the OS, ACL minimizes the number of packages, services, and potential entry points available to attackers and simplifies security management.-- **Automated node image updates**: ACL delivers weekly image-based updates that include the latest security patches and bug fixes. This approach keeps node OS versions consistent and current across the cluster and helps reduce exposure to known vulnerabilities.-- **Supply-chain trust**: Builds on Azure Linux’s signed packages and supply-chain processes, delivering clear provenance for system components.-- **Integration with Azure security features**: Native support for [Trusted Launch](/en-us/azure/aks/use-trusted-launch) and Secure Boot provides measured boot protections and attestation.-- **Open-source transparency**: Flatcar as well as many of the underlying technologies (dm-verity and SELinux) are upstream or open source, and Microsoft has tooling and contributions to support these features.+| Benefit | Description |+| --- | --- |+| **Layered OS security** | ACL combines an immutable OS, mandatory access controls, verified boot, and trusted build processes to protect nodes from boot through runtime. For details, see [ACL security features](/en-us/articles/azure-linux/azure-container-linux-security-features.md). |+| **Minimal container host** | ACL includes only the components required to run containers, reducing OS complexity and simplifying node management. |+| **Consistent node servicing** | Weekly image-based updates provide security patches and bug fixes while keeping the OS version consistent across each node image. |+| **Open-source transparency** | Flatcar as well as many of the underlying technologies (dm-verity and SELinux) are upstream or open source, and Microsoft has tooling and contributions to support these features. | -## Key features of ACL+## Capabilities and compatibility -The following key features distinguish ACL as a hardened, container-optimized OS for AKS:+ACL supports the following AKS capabilities: -- **Immutability**: The '/usr' directory is mounted as a read-only volume protected by dm-verity. At runtime, the kernel validates a signed root hash to detect and block tampering-- **Mandatory access control with SELinux**: ACL includes SELinux to enforce mandatory access control policies that restrict which processes can access sensitive system resources. Note that *SELinux is operating in enforcing mode by default. SELinux policies might evolve over time*.-- **Trusted Launch and Secure Boot**: ACL requires [Trusted Launch](/en-us/azure/virtual-machines/trusted-launch) with Secure Boot and vTPM, to ensure the integrity of the boot chain before the OS loads. This is achieved using a Unified Kernel Image (UKI), which bundles the kernel, initramfs, and kernel command line into a single signed artifact. During boot, the UKI is measured and recorded in the vTPM, ensuring integrity from the earliest stage. - **NVIDIA GPU node support**: ACL supports NVIDIA GPU-enabled node pools on AMD64 architectures, allowing you to run high-performance computing (HPC) and AI/ML workloads on AKS with a hardened, container-optimized OS. ACL doesn't support ARM64 architectures for GPU-enabled node pools.+- **FIPS**: ACL supports FIPS-enabled node pools. - **AMD64 and ARM64 architecture support**: ACL is available for both AMD64 and ARM64 architectures on AKS.-- **Sovereign Supply Chain Security**: ACL inherits Azure Linux’s secure build pipelines and signed Unified Kernel Images (UKIs).-- **[Node auto-provisioning](node-auto-provisioning)**: ACL supports node auto-provisioning (NAP).+- **[Node auto-provisioning](/en-us/azure/aks/node-auto-provisioning)**: ACL supports node auto-provisioning (NAP).+- **[Confidential VM](/en-us/azure/aks/use-cvm)**: ACL is available as a confidential VM (CVM) image for AKS, with a FIPS-enabled option. -Important+## Unsupported features++ACL doesn't currently support the following features: -If you're using **Azure Container Linux (ACL)** on AKS, make sure you review the following considerations and limitations:+- The `SecurityPatch` and `Unmanaged`[node OS upgrade channels](/en-us/azure/aks/auto-upgrade-node-os-image).+- [Generation 1 VMs](/en-us/azure/aks/aks-virtual-machine-sizes): You can't use VM sizes that only support Generation 1 with ACL.+- [Pod Sandboxing](/en-us/azure/aks/use-pod-sandboxing).+- A non-Trusted Launch variant. ACL requires Trusted Launch. -- ACL is generally available starting AKS v1.34.-- ACL requires [Trusted Launch](/en-us/azure/aks/use-trusted-launch) with Secure Boot and vTPM. Non-Trusted Launch variants aren't available.-- ACL on Arm64 requires Cobalt-based (v6) SKUs to enable Trusted Launch compatibility.-- `NodeImage` and `None` are the only supported [operating system (OS) upgrade channels](/en-us/azure/aks/auto-upgrade-node-os-image). `Unmanaged` and `SecurityPatch` are incompatible with ACL due to the immutable `/usr` directory.-- [Artifact Streaming](/en-us/azure/aks/artifact-streaming) isn't supported.-- [Pod Sandboxing](/en-us/azure/aks/use-pod-sandboxing) isn't supported.-- [Confidential Virtual Machines (CVMs)](/en-us/azure/aks/confidential-containers-overview) aren't supported.-- [Generation 1 VMs](/en-us/azure/aks/aks-virtual-machine-sizes#vm-support-on-aks) aren't supported.+If your existing cluster uses any of these unsupported features, you might not be able to add an ACL node pool to that cluster.  ## Feature roadmap -For more information, see the [Azure Linux Feature Roadmap](https://github.com/orgs/microsoft/projects/970/views/2).+Azure Linux publishes a [feature roadmap](https://github.com/orgs/microsoft/projects/970/views/2) that contains features that are in development and available for general availability (GA) and public preview.  ## OS migrations and upgrades with ACL

The pod must be allowed to connect to your chosen test destination.
