To learn more, see [Allow the metric families in your own Prometheus](container-network-observability-how-to#allow-the-metric-families-in-your-own-prometheus).++## Configure collection for a workload++The `ContainerNetworkMetric` resource is a single, shared configuration for your cluster. Set `metadata.name` to `container-network-metric`, exactly as shown in the following examples. Kubernetes requires this name. You can choose any name for the YAML file. In that file:++- `spec.filters` lists the metrics you want to configure.+- `metric` identifies a metric type, such as `dns` or `tcp`.+- `includeFilters` selects traffic to count for that metric.+- `excludeFilters` selects traffic not to count for that metric.++Start with include filters to select the application traffic you need. Add exclude filters only when you want to omit a subset of that selection. Use exclude-only filters when you want to keep broad collection but remove specific observations. Exclusions aren't required, but they take precedence when present.++For example, to collect DNS metrics for an application, add a `dns` entry and select the application's pods in its filters. This changes DNS metric collection without changing TCP or other metric types, provided you preserve their existing entries. This resource filters Hubble metrics; it isn't a filter for every node-level metric exported by the cluster.++For your first configuration, follow the application example below from start to finish. After that, choose another task:++| Task | Configuration |+| --- | --- |+| **Filter DNS requests and replies for a client** | Use `dns` with source and destination filters. See Select DNS requests and replies. |+| **Filter TCP metrics by workload** | Use `tcp` with pod or label selectors. See Select workloads by label. |+| **Filter HTTP metrics for an application** | Use `httpV2` with workload filters. See Select HTTP observations for an application. |+| **Filter an existing metric by identity** | See Filter flow metrics by security identity. |+| **Exclude a workload from drop metrics** | Use `drop` with an exclude filter. See Exclude a workload from drop metrics. |+| **See external destination IP addresses in metrics** | See Inspect TCP traffic to external destinations. |+| **See destination ports in metrics** | See Inspect destination ports. |++Filters choose which traffic contributes to each metric. They don't change the metric's labels, such as source pod or destination IP.++Separate metric entries are independent. If you omit a service-provided metric from the resource, it remains enabled without a CNM filter for that metric. The resource isn't an allow list of every metric the cluster can collect.++You can filter `dns`, `tcp`, `httpV2`, `flow`, and `drop` when the service has enabled those metrics on your cluster. Configuring a filter doesn't establish that the workload is generating observations for that metric. DNS observations require a DNS inspection policy and DNS traffic. HTTP observations require L7 enablement, an HTTP inspection policy applied to the workload, and HTTP traffic through that policy. The resource's filter status doesn't verify these policy and traffic prerequisites. Adding a filter doesn't turn on inspection.++For HTTP metrics, the case-sensitive configuration name is `httpV2`, not `http`. The `metric` field chooses which metric to filter. The optional `protocol` field limits the traffic to `tcp`, `udp`, or `dns`; it doesn't accept `http`.++### Choose the test workload++In the Bash terminal you use for the following commands, set these values. Replace the pod name and URL. Change `production` if you use a different namespace. Set `POD_PREFIX` to the beginning of your application's pod names, and choose a running `CLIENT_POD` whose name starts with that prefix. For example, `checkout-` matches `checkout-7f6d8b9c5-x2abc`, but not `payments-7f6d8b9c5-x2abc`.++```bash+NAMESPACE="production"+POD_PREFIX="checkout-"+CLIENT_POD="<running-pod-with-curl>"+TEST_URL="https://<approved-host>/"+kubectl get pod -n "$NAMESPACE" "$CLIENT_POD" -o wide+kubectl exec -n "$NAMESPACE" "$CLIENT_POD" -- curl --version ``` -### Get cluster credentials+Confirm that the pod is running and `curl` is available. For a pod with multiple containers, add `-c <container-name>` to each `kubectl exec` command. Keep this terminal open so the variables remain available. -Get your cluster credentials by using the [`az aks get-credentials`](/en-us/cli/azure/aks#az_aks_get_credentials) command:+### Check the existing configuration -```azurecli-az aks get-credentials --resource-group $RESOURCE_GROUP --name $CLUSTER_NAME --overwrite-existing+Read the current configuration before making changes:++```bash+kubectl get containernetworkmetric container-network-metric -o yaml ``` -## Configure custom resources for metrics filtering+If the command returns `NotFound`, use the new-resource instructions. For any other error, stop and resolve it before continuing. -Container network metrics filtering uses the `ContainerNetworkMetric` Custom Resource Definition (CRD) to define filtering rules. Only one CRD can exist per cluster, and changes take approximately 30 seconds to reconcile. If the CRD is not applied, all metrics will be collected.+If the command displays an existing resource, save a copy before making changes: -```azurecli+```bash+kubectl get containernetworkmetric container-network-metric \+  -o yaml > network-metrics-before.yaml+```++Important++Keep the metric entries and filters you still need. To configure another metric, add an entry under `spec.filters`. If that metric already has an entry, update that entry instead of adding a duplicate.++For example, if you already filter `dns` and want to enable `flows-to-world`, keep the `dns` entry and add a `flows-to-world` entry beside it. Don't replace the DNS configuration with the new example.++### Filter flow metrics for one application++This example counts flow observations that come from the selected application's pods. Other source pods don't match this filter. It changes only the `flow` metric. It doesn't enable the optional metrics or change traffic permissions.++#### If the resource doesn't exist++Run this Bash command to create `network-metrics.yaml`. Bash replaces `${NAMESPACE}` and `${POD_PREFIX}` with the values you set above:++```bash+cat > network-metrics.yaml <<EOF apiVersion: acn.azure.com/v1alpha1 kind: ContainerNetworkMetric metadata:-  name: : container-network-metric # Cluster scoped+  name: container-network-metric spec:   filters:-  - metric: flow-    includeFilters: # List of include filters-      - name: sample-filter # Filter name-        from:-          namespacedPod: # List of source namespace/pods. Prepend namespace with /-            - sample-namespace/sample-pod-          labelSelector: # Standard k8s label selector-            matchLabels:-              app: frontend-              k8s.io/namespace: sample-namespace-            matchExpressions:-              - key: environment-                operator: In-                values:-                  - production-                  - staging-          ip: # List of source IPs; can be CIDR-            - "192.168.1.10"-            - "10.0.0.1"-        to:-          namespacedPod:-            - sample-namespace2/sample-pod2-          labelSelector:-            matchLabels:-              app: backend-              k8s.io/namespace: sample-namespace2-            matchExpressions:-              - key: tier-                operator: NotIn-                values:-                  - dev-          ip:-            - "192.168.1.20"-            - "10.0.1.1"-        protocol: # List of protocols; can be tcp, udp, dns-          - tcp-          - udp-          - dns-        verdict: # List of verdicts; can be forwarded, dropped-          - forwarded-          - dropped-    metric: dns-    excludeFilters: # List of exclude filters-      - name: sample-filter # Filter name-        from:-          namespacedPod: # List of source namespace/pods. Prepend namespace with /-            - sample-namespace/sample-pod-          labelSelector: # Standard k8s label selector-            matchLabels:-              app: frontend-              k8s.io/namespace: sample-namespace+    - metric: flow+      includeFilters:+        - name: selected-application+          from:+            namespacedPod: ["${NAMESPACE}/${POD_PREFIX}"]+EOF ``` -The following table describes the fields in the custom resource definition:+For these example values, the selector is `production/checkout-`: the namespace must be exactly `production`, and the pod name must start with `checkout-`. Keep the pod-name prefix after `/`; omitting it selects every pod in that namespace. A full pod name also uses prefix matching, not an exact-name comparison. -| Field | Type | Description | Required |-| --- | --- | --- | --- |-| `filters.metric` | String | Name of the metric you would like to apply the filter on. This is mandatory. The supported values are `dns`, `flow`, `tcp`, `drop` | Mandatory |-| `includeFilters` or `excludeFilters` | []filter | A list of filters that define network flows to include. Each filter specifies the source, destination, protocol, and other matching criteria. You must have at least one include or exclude filter. | Mandatory |-| `filters.name` | String | The name of the filter. | Optional |-| `filters.protocol` | []string | The protocols to match for this filter. Valid values are `tcp`, `udp`, and `dns`. Because it's an optional parameter, if it isn't specified, logs with all protocols are included. | Optional |-| `filters.verdict` | []string | The verdict of the flow to match. Valid values are `forwarded` and `dropped`. Because it's an optional parameter, if it isn't specified, logs with all verdicts are included. | Optional |-| `filters.from` | Endpoint | Specifies the source of the network flow. Can include IP addresses, label selectors, and namespace/pod pairs. | Optional |-| `Endpoint.ip` | []string | It can be a single IP or a CIDR. | Optional |-| `Endpoint.labelSelector` | Object | A label selector is a mechanism to filter and query resources based on labels, so you can identify specific subsets of resources. A label selector can include two components: `matchLabels` and `matchExpressions`. Use `matchLabels` for straightforward matching by specifying a key/value pair (for example, `{"app": "frontend"}`). For more advanced criteria, use `matchExpressions`, where you define a label key, an operator (such as `In`, `NotIn`, `Exists`, or `DoesNotExist`), and an optional list of values. Ensure that the conditions in both `matchLabels` and `matchExpressions` are met, because they're logically combined by `AND`. If no conditions are specified, the selector matches all resources. To match none, leave the selector null. Carefully define your label selector to target the correct set of resources. | Optional |-| `Endpoint.namespacedPod` | []string | A list of namespace and pod pairs (formatted as `namespace/pod`) for matching the source. `name` should match the RegEx pattern `^.+$`. | Optional |-| `filters.to` | Endpoint | Specifies the destination of the network flow. Can include IP addresses, label selectors, or namespace/pod pairs. | Optional |-| `Endpoint.ip` | []string | It can be a single IP or a CIDR. | Optional |-| `Endpoint.labelSelector` | Object | A label selector to match resources based on their labels. | Optional |-| `Endpoint.namespacedPod` | []string | A list of namespace and pod pairs (formatted as `namespace/pod`) to match the destination. | Optional |--Apply the `ContainerNetworkMetric` custom resource to enable log collection at the cluster:+#### If the resource already exists -```azurecli-kubectl apply -f <crd.yaml>+Don't run the new-resource command. Copy the backup to a working file:++```bash+cp network-metrics-before.yaml network-metrics.yaml ``` -## Clean up and reset+Open the working file in your editor: -To clean up filtering configuration:+1. Keep `apiVersion`, `kind`, `metadata.name`, and `spec`, along with any user-managed labels and annotations you need. Remove `status` and server-generated metadata such as `resourceVersion`, `uid`, `creationTimestamp`, `managedFields`, and the `kubectl.kubernetes.io/last-applied-configuration` annotation.+2. Keep the existing entries under `spec.filters`.+3. If there's no `flow` entry, add the entry shown in the following example. Replace `production/checkout-` with your namespace and application pod-name prefix.+4. If `flow` already exists, review its include and exclude filters before editing it. To restrict it to this application, update that entry rather than adding a second `flow` entry. Coordinate any change to existing collection with the administrators who depend on it. -```azurecli-# Delete the CRD-kubectl delete ContainerNetworkMetric container-network-metric-```+For example, an existing configuration might contain only a DNS filter: -## Example filtering configuration+```yaml+apiVersion: acn.azure.com/v1alpha1+kind: ContainerNetworkMetric+metadata:+  name: container-network-metric+spec:+  filters:+    - metric: dns+      includeFilters:+        - from:+            namespacedPod: ["production/checkout-"]+``` -1. Create a basic filtering configuration that focuses on DNS metrics:+The complete configuration would look like this after adding the flow filter:  ```yaml-# basic-dns-filter.yaml apiVersion: acn.azure.com/v1alpha1 kind: ContainerNetworkMetric metadata:   name: container-network-metric spec:   filters:-    - metric: dns  # Supported: dns, flow, tcp, drop-      excludeFilters:+    - metric: dns+      includeFilters:         - from:-            namespacedPod: ["kube-system/coredns"]+            namespacedPod: ["production/checkout-"]+    - metric: flow+      includeFilters:+        - name: selected-application+          from:+            namespacedPod: ["production/checkout-"]+```++Both examples are complete resources. The second keeps the first example's DNS filter and adds a flow filter. When you edit your own configuration, preserve your actual DNS settings and any other metric entries. Keep the backup unchanged so you can refer to it during cleanup.++### Validate and apply the configuration++First, check whether the cluster accepts the YAML without saving changes:++```bash+kubectl apply --dry-run=server -f network-metrics.yaml+```++If the check fails, correct the reported error before continuing. If it succeeds, apply the file:++```bash+kubectl apply -f network-metrics.yaml+```++View the resource to check its status:++```bash+kubectl get containernetworkmetric container-network-metric -o yaml ``` -1. Configure filtering for TCP metrics with include and exclude filters:+Wait for the controller to process the change. Look for `status.state: CONFIGURED` and read `status.warnings`. If the state is `FAILED`, read `status.reason`, correct the file, and repeat the validation and apply steps. Configuration acceptance alone doesn't show that the agent is producing metrics; verify that next.++### Generate traffic and verify the result++1. For managed Prometheus, open the receiving **Azure Monitor workspace** in the Azure portal and select **Metrics**. Select **Add metric** &gt; **Add with editor**, choose that workspace as the scope, enter your PromQL query, and select **Run**. See [Metrics explorer with PromQL](/en-us/azure/azure-monitor/metrics/metrics-explorer). You don't need an Azure Managed Grafana instance.++    If you already use Grafana, you can use **Explore** with your cluster's Prometheus data source instead. For your own Prometheus server, use its query page. If the backend contains multiple clusters, add your backend's cluster-label selector to the query.+2. Before generating traffic, run this query. Replace the source value with your namespace and pod name; PromQL doesn't substitute Bash variables.++    ```promql+    hubble_flows_processed_total{source="production/<client-pod>"}+    ```++    Record the values and the time. The query can return multiple series with different labels. If no series exists yet, note that as your baseline.+3. In the Bash terminal where you set the workload variables, make one request:++    ```bash+    kubectl exec -n "$NAMESPACE" "$CLIENT_POD" -- \+      curl --fail --show-error --silent --output /dev/null \+        --write-out 'HTTP %{http_code}\n' \+        --connect-timeout 10 --max-time 20 "$TEST_URL"+    ```++    Check for a successful response from your approved endpoint. Resolve request failures before using the result to evaluate filtering.+4. Allow time for your configured Prometheus collection interval and ingestion delay, then run the same query again. Look for a new series or an increase in an existing counter for the test pod. The counter need not increase by exactly one: it counts observed flows, not application requests.++This step verifies collection for the selected pod. It doesn't by itself prove that all other traffic is excluded. Historical series can remain visible after filters change. To test exclusion, compare counter changes for an unselected workload while it generates known traffic, rather than expecting its old series to disappear.++If no new values appear, use Troubleshoot metric configuration. The alternative direct agent check can help distinguish agent collection from backend collection problems.++## DNS, TCP, HTTP, and drop filtering examples++Each example in this section is a complete `ContainerNetworkMetric` resource. Choose the example that fits your task, replace its workload names or labels, and save it as `network-metrics.yaml`.++Important++These examples are alternatives, not separate resources to apply one after another. They all update the same cluster-wide configuration. If the resource already exists, keep its other metric entries and filters in your file before applying a change. See the complete before-and-after example.++For each change, follow Validate and apply the configuration. Then use the same before-and-after check described in Generate traffic and verify the result, with traffic appropriate to the metric. Use your own workload names in both the filters and queries.++The selection examples use include filters only. The separate drop exclusion example shows how to keep broad collection while omitting a workload. For combining inclusion with an exception, see the filter reference.++### Select workloads by label++This configuration selects TCP metric observations from pods labeled `app: checkout`. Replace the label with an application-specific label used by your test workload. You don't need to exclude anything to select the application.++Important++In the current implementation, multiple label conditions are evaluated independently (OR), unlike the usual Kubernetes label-selector AND behavior. For example, adding `tier: frontend` would also select pods with that label even if they aren't labeled `app: checkout`. This example has no source namespace restriction. If needed, add `namespacedPod: ["production/"]` under the same `from` field. Replace `production` with your namespace. The namespace and label criteria must then both match.  ```yaml-# tcp-metrics-filter.yaml apiVersion: acn.azure.com/v1alpha1 kind: ContainerNetworkMetric metadata:@@ -200,44 +288,81 @@ spec:   filters:     - metric: tcp       includeFilters:-          - from:+        - from:             labelSelector:               matchLabels:-                tier: "frontend"-      excludeFilters:-        - to:-            namespacedPod: ["kube-system/metrics-server"]+                app: checkout ``` -1. Configure filtering for network flow metrics:+Confirm that the source pod has the selected label:++```bash+kubectl get pod -n "$NAMESPACE" "$CLIENT_POD" --show-labels+```++Generate TCP traffic by using the earlier `curl` command, and then query `hubble_tcp_flags_total` for the selected cluster and workload. This metric counts FIN, SYN, SYN-ACK, and RST flags on eligible forwarded or redirected observations. It doesn't count every TCP packet or unique connection.++### Select DNS requests and replies++Before using this example, configure [DNS visibility](how-to-apply-fqdn-filtering-policies) by applying a policy with DNS inspection rules to your workload. DNS metric observations are generated when the workload sends DNS traffic through that policy. Allowing TCP or UDP port 53 alone doesn't enable inspection. A `dns` metric filter doesn't apply or validate the required policy.++Use two filters to include DNS traffic in both directions. Replace `production/client-` with your client's namespace and pod-name prefix.  ```yaml-# flow-metrics-filter.yaml apiVersion: acn.azure.com/v1alpha1 kind: ContainerNetworkMetric metadata:   name: container-network-metric spec:   filters:-    - metric: flow+    - metric: dns       includeFilters:         - from:-            labelSelector:-              matchLabels:-                tier: "frontend"+            namespacedPod: ["production/client-"]+          protocol: ["dns"]         - to:-            labelSelector:-              matchLabels:-                tier: "backend"-      excludeFilters:-        - from:-            namespacedPod: ["default/test"]+            namespacedPod: ["production/client-"]+          protocol: ["dns"] ``` -1. Configure filtering for dropped packet metrics:+The first filter selects traffic sent by the client. The second selects traffic sent back to it. Either filter can match. Generate a DNS lookup from the selected pod using its installed DNS client, then inspect `hubble_dns_queries_total` and `hubble_dns_responses_total` in your metrics backend. Check the client in the source or destination labels as appropriate.++Changing DNS filters doesn't enable DNS inspection or change other metric types.++### Select HTTP observations for an application++Before using this example, complete [Set up Layer 7 (L7) policies with ACNS](how-to-apply-l7-policies?tabs=cilium). That guide explains how to enable L7 policies on the cluster with `--acns-advanced-networkpolicies L7` and apply an HTTP policy. FQDN filtering alone isn't sufficient for this HTTP example.++You generate HTTP metric observations when you apply an HTTP inspection policy to your workload and HTTP traffic passes through that policy. Enabling L7 on the cluster alone isn't sufficient. A `httpV2` filter selects those observations; it doesn't apply the policy or verify that the workload meets these prerequisites. Generate HTTP traffic and check `hubble_http_requests_total` separately to verify collection, including your Prometheus ingestion settings. The TCP example above doesn't require HTTP inspection.++Use the case-sensitive metric name `httpV2`. This example includes observations from or to pods whose names start with `web-` in the `production` namespace. Replace these names with your application's namespace and pod-name prefix. The `httpV2` handler counts HTTP response observations. Its filters use the observed response's source and destination. The exported source and destination context labels are then reversed to represent the request direction. Don't assume that a filter's `from` endpoint is the metric's exported `source` label.++```yaml+apiVersion: acn.azure.com/v1alpha1+kind: ContainerNetworkMetric+metadata:+  name: container-network-metric+spec:+  filters:+    - metric: httpV2+      includeFilters:+        - name: http-from-web+          from:+            namespacedPod: ["production/web-"]+        - name: http-to-web+          to:+            namespacedPod: ["production/web-"]+```++Generate an HTTP request that receives a response through the application's configured inspection path. Compare `hubble_http_requests_total` before and after the request, selecting the cluster and workload under investigation.++Adding `httpV2` filters doesn't enable HTTP inspection or decrypt HTTPS traffic. The HTTPS requests in the optional-metric example demonstrate TCP world and port metrics, not HTTP metric collection.++### Exclude a workload from drop metrics++This configuration excludes drop observations from pods whose names start with `load-test-` in the `production` namespace. Replace this selector with the test workload you want to exclude. Other workloads remain eligible for drop metric collection. Use this exclude-only approach when you want to retain broad drop monitoring but omit load-test observations, rather than select one application.  ```yaml-# drop-metrics-filter.yaml apiVersion: acn.azure.com/v1alpha1 kind: ContainerNetworkMetric metadata:@@ -247,13 +372,164 @@ spec:     - metric: drop       excludeFilters:         - from:-            namespacedPod: ["kube-system/"]+            namespacedPod: ["production/load-test-"]+```++This configuration doesn't prevent or cause packet drops. It changes which existing drop events contribute to `hubble_drop_total`. Verify it with known dropped test traffic in an approved test environment, not by disrupting a production workload.++## Filter flow metrics by security identity++A Cilium security identity is a numeric identifier assigned to an endpoint or endpoint category. It's not an Azure managed identity or a user identity. You can use it in a source or destination filter instead of selecting individual IP addresses. Check that the cluster supports identity filters:++```bash+kubectl explain containernetworkmetric.spec.filters.includeFilters.to.identities ``` -1. Configure filtering for multiple metric types in a single CRD:+The following example restricts flow metrics to TCP traffic going to world (external) identities from the checkout application. Save it as `network-metrics.yaml`, replacing `production/checkout-` with your namespace and application pod-name prefix. If the resource already exists, keep its other metric entries and update its existing `flow` entry.++```yaml+apiVersion: acn.azure.com/v1alpha1+kind: ContainerNetworkMetric+metadata:+  name: container-network-metric+spec:+  filters:+    - metric: flow+      includeFilters:+        - name: checkout-world-traffic+          from:+            namespacedPod: ["production/checkout-"]+          to:+            identities: [2, 9, 10]+          protocol: ["tcp"]+```++Identity `2` represents world, `9` represents world IPv4, and `10` represents world IPv6. Listing `2` doesn't automatically include the other two. Some external destinations have different identities and don't match this filter. The API accepts numeric values from `0` through `16777215`, not aliases such as `world`.++Validate, apply, and repeat the traffic and query steps from the first example. Use an approved external destination classified as world. This filter changes which flows are counted; it doesn't add destination IP labels to the flow metric. To see external destination IPs, use the optional metric in the following section.++## Enable additional metrics++Use a filtered entry under `spec.filters` to enable `flows-to-world` or `port-distribution` when the service doesn't already supply the metric. There's no separate enablement flag in this resource. Each example below is a complete configuration for one metric. Preserve existing metric entries before applying it.++If the service already enables a metric, CNM filters it without replacing its existing labels or options. The descriptions below show the service-owned options used when CNM adds a metric. Inspect the emitted labels when comparing results on a cluster with an existing configuration.++| Action | Metric added by your CNM entry | Metric already supplied by the service |+| --- | --- | --- |+| Add a filtered entry | Enable and filter the metric. | Filter the metric; preserve its service-provided labels and options. |+| Remove that entry | Disable the metric. | Keep the metric enabled without that entry's filters. |+| Delete CNM | Remove CNM-added metrics. | Restore service-provided collection without any CNM filters. |++To enable both metrics, include both entries under `spec.filters` in the same resource. The configuration used for the captured results shows both metrics together, with an existing DNS entry preserved.++### Inspect TCP traffic to external destinations++Use this configuration to select TCP traffic from checkout pods in `production` to destinations with a world identity. Replace `production/checkout-` with your namespace and application pod-name prefix.++```yaml+apiVersion: acn.azure.com/v1alpha1+kind: ContainerNetworkMetric+metadata:+  name: container-network-metric+spec:+  filters:+    - metric: flows-to-world+      includeFilters:+        - name: checkout-world-egress+          from:+            namespacedPod: ["production/checkout-"]+          to:+            identities: [2, 9, 10]+          protocol: ["tcp"]+          verdict: ["forwarded"]+```++For a metric newly enabled through CNM, the service uses SYN-only counting: eligible non-reply TCP SYN observations to world destinations. It doesn't count UDP traffic. This example further restricts observations to forwarded traffic. Repeated SYN observations can increase the counter more than once for a connection attempt, so the counter isn't a count of successful connections.++Follow Validate and apply the configuration, then repeat the earlier baseline, `curl`, and query steps with this metric. Use the same `$NAMESPACE`, `$CLIENT_POD`, and `$TEST_URL` values, with a destination classified as world.++Query `hubble_flows_to_world_total` in Prometheus. For a workspace that contains multiple clusters, select the cluster under investigation before comparing results. Replace the source value below with your namespace and pod name:++```promql+hubble_flows_to_world_total{source="production/<client-pod>"}+```++Look for the selected source pod, the destination IP, and new observations from the test. Source and destination labels come from the service-managed contexts, not from adding identity filters. A destination assigned a different identity won't match the example.++### Inspect destination ports++Use this complete configuration to examine TCP and UDP destination ports used by checkout pods. Replace `production/checkout-` with your namespace and application pod-name prefix. If you already enabled `flows-to-world` and want to keep it, retain that entry in this file before applying it.++```yaml+apiVersion: acn.azure.com/v1alpha1+kind: ContainerNetworkMetric+metadata:+  name: container-network-metric+spec:+  filters:+    - metric: port-distribution+      includeFilters:+        - name: checkout-ports+          from:+            namespacedPod: ["production/checkout-"]+          protocol: ["tcp", "udp"]+```++Validate and apply the file using the earlier steps. Record a baseline, generate TCP traffic with the earlier `curl` command, and inspect the destination ports. Replace the source value with your namespace and pod name:++```promql+hubble_port_distribution_total{source="production/<client-pod>"}+```++The `protocol` and `port` labels identify the protocol and destination port. The metric counts forwarded or redirected traffic that the agent identifies as not being a reply. Dropped traffic and traffic with unknown reply status aren't counted. A `verdict: ["dropped"]` filter won't change this behavior.++An HTTPS request normally produces TCP/443 observations. UDP/53 observations can also appear if the pod performs DNS lookups over UDP; cached resolution might not produce new DNS traffic.++### Check metrics directly at the agent++Use this check if the backend query has no data or you want the terminal output shown in the following screenshots. It reads metrics directly from the Cilium agent on the test pod's node. It doesn't verify that Prometheus has collected them. You need permission to list pods and port-forward in `kube-system`, plus local `curl`.++In the terminal containing your test workload variables, find its node and list the Cilium pods on that node:++```bash+NODE=$(kubectl get pod -n "$NAMESPACE" "$CLIENT_POD" \+  -o jsonpath='{.spec.nodeName}')+kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=cilium \+  --field-selector "spec.nodeName=$NODE" -o wide+```++Stop if either command fails or no Cilium pod is listed. Set the name returned by the command, then start the port-forward:++```bash+CILIUM_POD="<cilium-pod-on-the-test-node>"+kubectl -n kube-system port-forward --address 127.0.0.1 \+  "pod/$CILIUM_POD" 19965:9965+```++Leave this terminal running. In a second Bash terminal, set the exact source label for your test pod and fetch the metrics:++```bash+SOURCE="<namespace>/<client-pod>"+date -u '+Scrape time (UTC): %Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ'+curl --fail --silent --show-error --max-time 15 \+  http://127.0.0.1:19965/metrics > agent-metrics.prom &&+grep -E '^hubble_(flows_processed|flows_to_world|port_distribution)_total[{]' \+  agent-metrics.prom | grep -F "source=\"$SOURCE\""+```++If `curl` reports an error, check the port-forward and whether the agent exposes metrics on port 9965. If it succeeds but no matching lines appear, check the source value, selected agent, metric configuration, and test traffic. Don't interpret an empty result as proof that filtering works.++Repeat the scrape before and after new traffic to compare counters. Keep the UTC time and complete labels so you compare the same series. Press **Ctrl+C** in the first terminal when you finish the port-forward.++### Example configuration and captured results++The following example shows the configuration used to collect both metrics from the `cnm-capture-client` pod in the `cnm-docs` namespace on a Cilium cluster. The test generated a DNS lookup and eight HTTPS requests to `https://www.microsoft.com`. All eight HTTPS requests returned HTTP 200.++#### Custom resource used for the test++This is the complete applied configuration, with server-generated metadata and status omitted. The existing `dns` entry was kept; the test added `flows-to-world` and `port-distribution` to the same resource.  ```yaml-# multi-metrics-filter.yaml apiVersion: acn.azure.com/v1alpha1 kind: ContainerNetworkMetric metadata:@@ -262,57 +538,150 @@ spec:   filters:     - metric: dns       includeFilters:-        - protocol: ["dns"]-      excludeFilters:-        - from:-            namespacedPod: ["kube-system/*"]-    - metric: tcp+        - name: dns-from-demo-client+          from:+            namespacedPod: ["pets/acns-panel-client-"]+        - name: dns-to-demo-client+          to:+            namespacedPod: ["pets/acns-panel-client-"]+    - metric: flows-to-world       includeFilters:-        - protocol: ["tcp"]-        - from:-            labelSelector:-              matchLabels:-                environment: "production"-    - metric: flow-      excludeFilters:-        - from:-            namespacedPod: ["default/debug-*"]-    - metric: drop+        - name: cnm-docs-world-egress+          from:+            namespacedPod: ["cnm-docs/cnm-capture-client"]+          to:+            identities: [2, 9, 10]+          protocol: ["tcp"]+          verdict: ["forwarded"]+    - metric: port-distribution       includeFilters:-        - reason: ["Policy denied", "Invalid"]+        - name: cnm-docs-destination-ports+          from:+            namespacedPod: ["cnm-docs/cnm-capture-client"]+          protocol: ["tcp", "udp"] ``` -## Best practices+The world filter selects forwarded TCP observations from the test client to destinations with a world identity. The port filter selects TCP and UDP observations from the same client. Pod names in `namespacedPod` are matched as prefixes; the test used a single pod with this name. -- Ensure you do not have conflicting include and exclude filter on the CRD.-- Leverage Kubernetes label selectors for flexible filtering.-- Always validate filtering configurations in development or staging-- Regularly review filtered metrics to ensure important data isn't lost.-- Remember that only one CRD can exist per cluster.+The `dns` entry selects a different workload from an earlier configuration. It isn't required to enable either optional metric, including UDP/53 observations in `port-distribution`. -## Troubleshooting+Important -### Common issues+This example uses the test cluster's pod and namespace names. Replace them with your own names before using it. If your cluster already has this resource, add or update only the metric entries you need and keep the other settings. -**Issue**: CRD configuration not applied+After the controller processed the changes, the resource reported `status.state: CONFIGURED`. It also warned that each optional metric could increase the number of time series and the cost of storing them. Both metrics were also verified in the configuration used by the agent before traffic was generated. To inspect your resource's state and warnings, run: -**Solution**: Check that the feature flag is registered and only one CRD exists:+```bash+kubectl get containernetworkmetric container-network-metric -o yaml+``` -```azurecli-# Verify feature registration-az feature show --namespace "Microsoft.ContainerService" --name "AdvancedNetworkingDynamicMetricsPreview"+#### World metric result -# Check existing CRDs-kubectl get ContainerNetworkMetric+The following screenshot shows a direct agent scrape at **16:41:33 UTC on November 2, 2026**. For source `cnm-docs/cnm-capture-client`, the `hubble_flows_to_world_total` sample shows the documentation address `203.0.113.10`, protocol `TCP`, verdict `FORWARDED`, and value **8**.++[![Terminal screenshot of hubble_flows_to_world_total showing eight forwarded TCP observations from cnm-docs/cnm-capture-client to the documentation address 203.0.113.10.](media/advanced-container-networking-services/hubble-flows-to-world-metric.png)](media/advanced-container-networking-services/hubble-flows-to-world-metric.png#lightbox)++*World metric output for the client selected by the `cnm-docs-world-egress` filter.*++The destination IP in the screenshot and sample description has been replaced with `203.0.113.10`, an address reserved for documentation. For your own tests, use an approved, reachable destination rather than this example address.++#### Destination-port result++The following screenshot shows a direct agent scrape at **16:43:28 UTC on November 2, 2026**, using the same source pod and configuration.++[![Terminal screenshot of hubble_port_distribution_total showing TCP port 443 with value 52 and two UDP port 53 series with values 24 and 34 for cnm-docs/cnm-capture-client.](media/advanced-container-networking-services/hubble-destination-port-metric.png)](media/advanced-container-networking-services/hubble-destination-port-metric.png#lightbox)++*Destination-port output for the client selected by the `cnm-docs-destination-ports` filter.*++| Protocol | Destination port | Destination label | Counter value |+| --- | --- | --- | --- |+| TCP | 443 | Empty: no destination pod metadata | 52 |+| UDP | 53 | `kube-system/coredns-5bf45f87d-dqpt2` | 24 |+| UDP | 53 | `kube-system/coredns-5bf45f87d-rljcr` | 34 |++All three series have `traffic_direction="egress"`. The empty destination label on the TCP/443 series is expected for an external destination without pod metadata.++These cumulative counters count observations, not unique requests or connections. The test traffic ran from **15:09:13 to 15:09:48 UTC**, before the screenshots were captured. The timestamps in the screenshots identify the scrapes, not the traffic interval. Values and destination addresses can differ in another run.++These screenshots show that the agent produced the metrics. They don't show whether Azure Monitor received the metrics or Grafana displayed them. Check your Prometheus backend separately as described in the preceding procedures.++## Filter reference++| Field | Description |+| --- | --- |+| **`spec.filters`** | List of metrics to filter. Include at least one entry. Use each metric name only once. |+| **`metric`** | Metric types covered in this guide: `flow`, `dns`, `drop`, `httpV2`, `tcp`, `flows-to-world`, and `port-distribution`. |+| **`includeFilters`** | Traffic to include for this metric. |+| **`excludeFilters`** | Traffic to exclude for this metric. |+| **`name`** | Optional name for a metric filter. A name alone doesn't select traffic. |+| **`from`, `to`** | Select where traffic comes from or goes to, using `namespacedPod`, `ip`, `labelSelector`, or `identities`. |+| **`labelSelector`** | In the current implementation, separate `matchLabels` entries and `matchExpressions` are alternatives (OR), not combined requirements (AND). See Select workloads by label. |+| **`identities`** | Numeric Cilium identities from `0` through `16777215`. Values in a list are alternatives. |+| **`protocol`** | `tcp`, `udp`, or `dns`. |+| **`verdict`** | `forwarded` or `dropped`. |++Each metric entry needs at least one include or exclude filter. Every filter must specify traffic-selection criteria, such as a pod name or protocol.++- Within one filter, different populated criteria must match together (AND): source and destination selectors, protocol, and verdict. Different selector fields on the same endpoint, such as `namespacedPod` and `labelSelector`, must also match together. For example, `namespacedPod: ["production/checkout-"]` under `from`, together with `protocol: ["tcp"]`, selects only TCP traffic from checkout pods in `production`.+- Values within a `namespacedPod`, `ip`, `identities`, `protocol`, or `verdict` list are alternatives (OR). For example, `protocol: ["tcp", "udp"]` matches either protocol.+- Within each endpoint's `labelSelector`, every `matchLabels` entry and every `matchExpressions` item becomes a separate selector. Any one can match (OR). Adding another label condition doesn't require both labels.+- With multiple include filters, traffic can match any one of them.+- If traffic matches an exclude filter, it isn't counted even if it also matches an include filter.++For example, an include filter for `production/checkout-` and an exclude filter for `production/checkout-load-test-` selects checkout pods except those whose names start with `checkout-load-test-`. If you provide only exclude filters, the metric continues to count other traffic that it normally counts.++For world traffic, identity `2` represents world, `9` represents world IPv4, and `10` represents world IPv6. Listing `2` doesn't expand to all three. Use the numeric identity that matches the observed traffic; not every external endpoint necessarily has a world identity.++For DNS and HTTP metrics, configure protocol inspection separately. A metric filter alone doesn't make DNS or HTTP details visible.++## Troubleshoot metric configuration++| Symptom | Action |+| --- | --- |+| **The command returns `Forbidden` or a connection error.** | Check your permissions, current Kubernetes context, and cluster connection. These errors don't mean the resource is missing. Resolve the error before changing the configuration. |+| **The API rejects the YAML file.** | Use the resource name `container-network-metric`. Check the metric name and identity range, and include at least one filter that selects traffic. |+| **The resource reports `FAILED`.** | Read `status.reason`. Check for duplicate metric entries or filters without traffic criteria. |+| **A warning mentions cardinality or ingestion cost.** | Additional metrics can create more time series and increase storage costs. Start with a small set of workloads and check how much data is collected. |+| **A warning says a metric isn't in the base configuration.** | Check the cluster's managed metric configuration. This warning isn't a check of whether the workload has the required inspection policy or is generating traffic. |+| **The resource is `CONFIGURED`, but no new observations appear.** | Filter status doesn't verify observation generation. For DNS, apply a DNS inspection policy and generate lookups. For HTTP, enable L7, apply an HTTP inspection policy, and generate HTTP traffic through it. Then check traffic selection, metric-specific counting behavior, and the Prometheus scrape pipeline. |+| **The agent shows samples, but the backend doesn't.** | Check scrape configuration, ingestion delay, cluster selection, and backend label names. An agent scrape doesn't verify backend ingestion. |+| **Old series from excluded workloads are still visible.** | Compare new counter changes during controlled traffic. Filtering doesn't delete historical samples or guarantee immediate removal of existing series. |+| **Label filtering includes more workloads than expected.** | Multiple label entries match independently (OR). Check for pods matching any entry, including in other namespaces. Use one application-specific label condition and combine it with a namespace/pod selector when needed. |+| **An optional metric remains after its entry is removed.** | Check whether the service supplies it. Removing CNM filters doesn't disable a service-provided metric. |+| **World or port counters don't increase.** | Verify destination identity and handler eligibility. World SYN-only counting doesn't include UDP; port distribution doesn't include dropped or reply observations. |++The service manages metric labels. This resource configures filters rather than custom label sets.++## Restore the previous configuration++If the resource existed before you started, use the saved copy to identify the settings you changed. Undo only your test changes. Keep any changes that other administrators made since you saved the copy.++- Removing a `flows-to-world` or `port-distribution` entry disables it only if that entry enabled it. A metric already supplied by the service remains enabled.+- Removing a default metric's filter entry restores its default collection behavior. It doesn't disable the default metric.++Restore your edits in the working manifest, validate it, and apply it using Validate and apply the configuration. Recheck status and fresh observations. Removing restrictions can increase collection, so coordinate restoration with the resource's other users.++If you created the resource for this example and no one else now depends on it, delete it to restore the service's default metric configuration:++```bash+kubectl delete containernetworkmetric container-network-metric ``` -**Issue**: Metrics still showing after applying excludeFilters+Previously collected series remain subject to your backend's retention policy.++## Best practices -**Solution**: Remember that preexisting metrics persist in Prometheus. You may need to wait for new metrics to be generated to see the filtering effects.+- Test filters on a small workload before applying them broadly.+- Review both include and exclude lists; exclusions take precedence.+- Use label or pod selectors for workloads and numeric identities for identity-based selection.+- Review ingestion volume when enabling optional metrics.+- Coordinate changes with other cluster administrators. The resource is shared across the cluster, not limited to one namespace.  ## Limitations -- This feature is specifically designed for Cilium data planes only-- Only one `ContainerNetworkMetric` CRD can exist per cluster-- Preexisting metrics persist in Prometheus; new filtering rules apply to newly generated metrics-- Requires Kubernetes version 1.32 or later+- Metric filtering requires the Cilium data plane and the prerequisites described earlier in this article.+- Only one `ContainerNetworkMetric` resource is supported per cluster.+- Multiple conditions within one endpoint's `labelSelector` are evaluated as alternatives, not as Kubernetes-style AND requirements. This evaluation method applies to both include and exclude filters.+- Filters affect new observations; historical data can remain visible.+- The service continues to manage metric dimensions.+- Filters can't make a metric count traffic that its handler excludes.

You configure workload enrollment, service participation, and the underlying connectivity required by your topology. -The following diagram illustrates the architectural layers of Azure Kubernetes Application Network and how they interact with each other and with your AKS clusters:+The following diagram shows the management plane, managed control plane, and data plane, with their separate API, control, and application traffic paths: -[![Screenshot of a diagram illustrating the architectural layers of Azure Kubernetes Application Network and how they interact with each other and with AKS clusters.](media/architecture/application-network-architecture.png)](media/architecture/application-network-architecture.png#lightbox)+[![Diagram of the Application Network management plane, managed control plane, and AKS member data plane, with separate control and application traffic paths.](media/architecture/application-network-architecture.svg)](media/architecture/application-network-architecture.svg#lightbox)  ## Management plane  The management plane is the Azure resource provider that handles all Application Network resource operations. When you create an Application Network resource or join a member cluster, the management plane validates the request, provisions supporting Azure resources such as Azure Key Vault for certificate storage, and orchestrates the creation of a regional control plane for the member. -You interact with the management plane through the Azure CLI ([`az appnet`](/en-us/cli/azure/appnet)) or the ARM API. The management plane coordinates all downstream provisioning so that control plane and data plane components are deployed without manual intervention.+You interact with the management plane through the Azure CLI ([`az appnet`](/en-us/cli/azure/appnet)) or the ARM API. The management plane coordinates all downstream provisioning so that control plane and data plane components deploy without manual intervention.  ## Control plane -The control plane is fully managed infrastructure that runs outside your AKS cluster. When a member cluster joins an Application Network, a dedicated control plane is provisioned in the same Azure region as the member cluster, keeping latency between control and data plane components low.+The control plane is fully managed infrastructure that runs outside your AKS cluster. When a member cluster joins an Application Network, the service provisions a dedicated control plane in the same Azure region as the member cluster, keeping latency between control and data plane components low. For Fleet Manager, OCIRepository support is especially important because it aligns closely with registry-first application delivery workflows.  An `OCIRepository` points to a container registry location that contains an OCI artifact, such as a versioned application bundle or Kustomize package. This pattern is useful when you want immutable, signed, and centrally managed artifacts instead of directly syncing a Git repo.
